title: Jeremiah 4:1–4
context: The LORD answers the confession of 3:22–25 with conditions. In 4:1–2 he addresses Israel: if they return to him and put away their abominations, they will not be removed, and they will swear “As the LORD lives” in truth, justice, and righteousness, so that the nations bless themselves in him (an echo, by reference, of the promises to Abraham in Genesis 12:3; 22:18). In 4:3–4 the LORD turns to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: “Break up your fallow ground” (the same words appear in Hosea 10:12) and “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart,” lest his wrath burn like unquenchable fire. Many readers take these verses as closing the unit that began in 2:1. The command to circumcise the heart echoes Deuteronomy 10:16, where the site already sets out Arminian and Reformed readings of a command to do what God elsewhere promises to do (Deuteronomy 30:6; compare Jeremiah 31:33; 32:39). The notes here point to that discussion rather than repeat it. Both traditions agree that the command is real, that grace is necessary, and that outward ritual without a changed heart is not enough (compare 9:25–26; Romans 2:29).

verses.text: “If you will return, Israel,” says the LORD, “if you will return to me, and if you will put away your abominations out of my sight; then you will not be removed;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “If you will return, Israel … if you will return to me, and … put away your abominations … then you will not be removed.” Arminian readers see genuinely conditional language: covenant blessing depends on a response that the people, enabled by grace, can make or refuse. The repeated “if” makes the invitation sincere and urgent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the conditions are real and binding, and they hold that God works in his people to meet the conditions he sets, so that the call is the means of his grace. Shared ground: both traditions read return as more than words, requiring abominations to be put away, and both hear the LORD answering the confession of 3:22–25.

verses.text: and you will swear, ‘As the LORD lives,’ in truth, in justice, and in righteousness. The nations will bless themselves in him, and they will glory in him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Sworn oaths “As the LORD lives,” in truth, justice, and righteousness, will lead the nations to bless themselves in him, echoing the promises to Abraham (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). Arminian readers see Israel’s faithfulness as the means through which blessing reaches the nations, a vocation Israel was able to fulfill or neglect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same echo of Abraham and stress that God’s purpose to bless the nations stands firm, ultimately fulfilled in Christ, even when Israel fails. Shared ground: both traditions see Israel’s faithfulness tied to the nations’ blessing, and both read the oath formula as worship of the true God, not ritual words alone.

verses.text: For the LORD says to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Judah and Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns” (the first words also in Hosea 10:12). Arminian readers see a call to prepare the heart, a real human responsibility enabled by grace, so that the seed of God’s word is not wasted on unready soil.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image exposing hearts hardened like unplowed ground, which need God’s work for any lasting growth, while the command remains the means God uses. Shared ground: both traditions read the farming image as a call to repentance before new sowing, and both see sowing among thorns as reform without heart change.

verses.text: Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.
verses.arminianNotes: “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart.” The site’s fuller discussion is at Deuteronomy 10:16. Arminian readers see a real command implying a grace-enabled response, and they read God’s promised heart circumcision (Deuteronomy 30:6) as received through cooperation that can be refused; the warning of unquenchable wrath underlines that refusal is possible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers, as at Deuteronomy 10:16, hear the command exposing inability, with God promising to do what he commands through effectual renewal (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 31:33; 32:39). Shared ground: both traditions affirm that the command is real, that grace is necessary, and that outward ritual without inward change cannot avert judgment.
